newsitem.title: USA: Rising condensate output seen affecting oil market.
newsitem.headline: Rising condensate output seen affecting oil market.

text.p: Rising output of condensates, particularly those related to increased natural gas production, could have a significant impact on the oil market over the next decade, some industry experts maintain.

Condensates, light liquid hydrocarbons which are separated by cooling and other means, traditionally have been a byproduct of crude oil production and been easy to blend and integrate with the existing crude infrastructure.

But thanks to rising natural gas production in the last decade, condensates are increasingly appearing as a byproduct of natgas production whose fields are often separate from crude fields and infrastructure.
"It is one of the potentially more important developments in the oil world," said Kevin Lindemer, an analyst at Boston-based Cambridge Energy Research Associates (CERA).

Between now and the year 2010, condensates will grow from three million barrels per day (bpd) (about four percent of current demand for liquids) to about 7.5 million bpd (eight percent of forecast demand), with much of the growth coming from natural gas production, according to CERA forecasts.
CERA's Lindemer maintains the new origins of condensate limit possibilities for blending with crude, forcing the industry to reevaluate how it markets the increasingly important by-product.
"There is condensate coming up that is not associated with crude so if you want to blend it with crude you have to transport it to crude," Lindemer said.
Much of the concern about what to do with the growing supplies is focused on the varying quality of different condensate streams, analysts said.
Specifically, analysts note that condensates coming out of the Middle East tend to be parafinic, or rather pure and very well suited for processing into petrochemicals.

But supplies coming out of Latin America tend to be naphthenic, or more suited as a feedstock for motor fuels like gasoline, and if earmarked for the petrochemical sector, more in need of expensive processing.
"The biggest question is going to be impurities, and the more parafinic it is the better," said Mike Gelardi, a petrochemical analyst at DeWitt & Co in Houston.
He said different condensate streams around the world suffer from various impurities such as heavy metals, or "hydrocarbon tails" that need processing to be removed.

"The quality issue for condensates still remains a significant unanswered question," CERA's Lindemer said. "The new condensates could produce a product mix that is not in line with the market," with the result that the new condensate supply could put downward pressure on light-to-heavy crude spreads.

That is already a major feature of the oil market this year as more Latin American and offshore Gulf of Mexico heavy crude supply hits the market. The discount for heavy "sour" crude in the U.S., for example, went from around $1.50 at the start of the year to about $3.00 last month.
"As the qualities of the condensate materialize on the market, investment decisions will be made based on that," Lindemer said.
